//: X3F — Firebase project configuration.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL. The database rules were published by hand through the
console, which means firebase/database.rules.json and the rules actually being
enforced could drift apart with nothing anywhere to notice. Declaring them here makes
the repo the source and `firebase deploy --only database` the way they ship.
WHAT IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: any `rewrites` block. This is a MULTI-PAGE site, not a
single-page app. The reflex `{ source: '**', destination: '/index.html' }` would serve
the launcher for every unknown path, so a typo would look like a working page and
X3F_Pair.html would still resolve after being deleted. Let 404s be 404s.
`cleanUrls` is off for a harder reason than taste: it 301s /X3F_Pair.html to
/X3F_Pair, and every link in this app — plus the copy baked into the TV bundle by
tools/sync-from-web.py — is written with the extension. Turning it on would put a
redirect in front of every navigation in the app, the pairing deep link included.

//headers: TWO RULES OF THIS BLOCK, BOTH ESTABLISHED BY EXPERIMENT AGAINST A PREVIEW CHANNEL
RATHER THAN BY READING, because both were wrong on the first attempt:
1. MATCHING IS AGAINST THE REQUEST PATH, NOT THE FILE SERVED. '/index.html' and '/'
are different paths even though they return the same bytes, so a glob written for
the file misses the URL a person actually types. The bare root needs its own rule,
and the literal source that matches it is exactly "/" — "@(/)" matches nothing at
all, and "/*" would also sweep in every top-level file.
2. FOR A GIVEN HEADER KEY, THE LAST MATCHING RULE WINS. So these run general to
specific and the order is load-bearing: sw.js sits at the bottom because the
generic *.js rule above it would otherwise overwrite its Cache-Control. Moving a
rule up this list is a silent behaviour change.

//: Defence in depth for a page that holds a live pairing code in its fragment. The
fragment never reaches a server, but a referrer can still leak the page it came
from, and nothing here has any reason to be framed.
Art is not immutable — tools/art/build.py can regenerate a plate under the same
name — but it changes rarely and is the heaviest thing on the site. A week is
long enough to be worth having and short enough that a regenerated movement plate
reaches a phone without anyone clearing anything.
Fonts are the one genuinely immutable thing here: the filenames come out of the
subsetting step and carry their own identity (sora-var-latin.woff2), so a change
to the type is a change to the filename. A year, and no revalidation at all.
Everything hashless and small revalidates instead. `no-cache` does not mean 'do
not cache' — it means 'ask before reusing', so the ordinary answer is a 304 with
no body. The whole site is 2.6 MB and the service worker means most of these are
never requested twice anyway, so asking costs close to nothing, and what it buys
is that a deploy is visible on the next reload rather than whenever some cache
happens to expire.
THE BARE ROOT, which the rule above does not match and which is the one URL that
gets read off a television and typed into a phone. Without this it inherited
Firebase's default of max-age=3600: a full hour of stale launcher at the app's
front door.
THE SERVICE WORKER, LAST SO IT WINS.
A HONEST NOTE, because the first version of this comment overclaimed and someone
will otherwise repeat the overclaim. This header is NOT what makes service-worker
updates work, and GitHub Pages' inability to set it was NOT the reason hosting
moved. Browsers already bypass the HTTP cache for a worker's own script:
ServiceWorkerRegistration defaults updateViaCache to 'imports', which exempts the
top-level script. Pages' flat max-age=600 would not have delayed an update.
What this header actually buys is the ONE hole that default really leaves: a new
worker installing within the cache window can precache stale bytes into its fresh
cache name, at which point activate() deletes the good cache and the stale copy
is what survives. web/sw.js already closes that itself with
`new Request(u, {cache: 'reload'})` in its install handler. So this is a second
lock on a door that has one — cheap, and worth having on the file whose whole job
is deciding what everyone else sees.
It does NOT replace the cache-name stamp in the deploy workflow. Those fix
genuinely different halves: a stamp makes a re-fetched sw.js DIFFER in bytes, so
the browser installs it and its activate() drops the previous cache. A header
cannot do that, and no header on any host ever could.
